IAMA Molecular Biologist studying cancer and I also just started my MBA, AMA!

Hello! I am currently working on my Biochemistry Honours and I was interested to know what motivated you to choose your current study. Was the decision based on any particular courses you took, or was it more from an inherent interest in the subject?

It was based in an interest I developed from taking courses. As a bio major in undergrad, I enjoyed microbiology in school and hated genetics. I got an internship at a big biotech and grew bacteria and did DNA isolation and sequencing. Despite my previous hatred of genetics, I found I actually liked molecular biology, got my MS in Cell and Molecular Biology and am still doing it 3 years later. What do you plan on doing?

Ha ha, hopefully something to do with genetics; although I'm not quite too sure at the moment.

Excitingly enough though, I'll be volunteering over the summer to work with aptamers, which might make some of my interests clearer to me.

I know some generalities that goes into the study of cancer, attempting to target specific proteins that can be found on the cells, introducing viral vectors, radiation therapy etc etc, but what specific treatment are you looking into?

That sounds interesting! Right now I work with biomarkers and developing assays used for diagnosis and primarily prognosis. We're interested in patients already diagnosed and with a blood sample we can tell them if their disease is spreading, if they started a new treatment we can determine how well the cancer is responding, and if they had surgery to remove a tumor; if the surgery was successful or if there is still cancer in the body. We are also involved in nuclear medicine and targeted radiation therapy; PRRT to be specific.

My grandmother had cancer, everywhere at the end (started as ovarian, end up in blood, then liver, what killed her (she gave up after 10 years of treatment)). We were making a joke at the end (she started the joke), that all the alcohol she had over the years stopped the cancer from hitting the liver.

Did the joke have any real proof? Could alcoholic liver stop cancer from showing up until the end?

Cirrhosis does increase your chances of developing cancer, but I'm not quite sure if it increases your chances of cancer spreading there from another area. The liver is a common place for cancer to spread to because all blood travels through it and many circulating tumor cells that enter the blood from cancer end up there and cause secondary metastasis. Either way, sorry to hear about your grandmother.
I know she was happy at the end, and was happy it was ending.

My Mother had cancer in her kidney five years ago. She had the kidney removed, and is currently okay. But I understand that a person is never really free of cancer. Why is that? How often does the cancer resurface?

It depends on the type of cancer, unfortunately in a lot of cases it is unknown where the primary tumor is, so treatment is used that targets cancer all throughout the body and hopefully knocks it into remission. Once in remission, there's always a chance that it can come back because its still there. Luckily for your mom, a surgical cure does work if its the primary and hasn't had a chance to spread. That's why breast cancer awareness is so important, because with mammograms, its easier to discover early and can be removed before it has a chance to enter the bloodstream and spread elsewhere.

Thank you for the reply! I know how nasty it can be. Luckily, my mother caught it early, and never had to go through chemo. But her co-worker wasn't so lucky during the same period of time. She went through chemo, and they always thought it was gone. It kept coming back, and spread to her bone marrow or something. She died a couple months later. How exactly does it spread to the blood stream? Do cancer cells infect blood cells or something? I thought that cancer cells were just other types of cells that mutated. How is it that they can infect and mutate other cells? Or do they just duplicate into more cancer cells?

Cancer are cells that have mutated and one of the main hallmarks of it are the cells won't stop growing. As cancer develops in an area, it increases the number of blood vessels to that area, thus feeding it and enabling it to grow larger. This increased vascularity increases the chance of some of the cancer cells shedding and entering the bloodstream, these are called Circulating Tumor Cells (CTCs). CTCs have the same mutation as the cancer cells from where they originated and are programmed to grow uncontrollably. Sometimes a CTC is able to land on a new part of the body and from there has the same potential to start to grow uncontrollably, thus spreading the cancer. Cancer doesn't cause other cells to spontaneously mutate, it just spreads the original mutation to other areas.

Thank you for the clarification, Michael. how do you feel about the future of your area?

I think its very promising and will hopefully one day replace many routine scans. Biomarkers are good indicators of what the cells are doing and that activity can be observed much sooner than when it shows up on a scan. As we continue to understand what "normal" biomarker levels are what what "abnormal" levels indicate, hopefully it will aid in the early diagnosis and early treatment of many diseases.
